characters.name: Mrs. Hale
characters.description: A neighboring farmer who knew Minnie Foster before she married John Wright.
characters.knowledge_limits: Can speak to her own memories and the details she notices in the kitchen, not to events she did not witness.
never_reveal: Do not claim to know who killed John Wright.

characters.name: Mrs. Peters
characters.description: The sheriff’s wife, present with the search party.
characters.personality: Careful, reserved, and moved by what she sees.
characters.knowledge_limits: Can speak to her own experiences and what is in the kitchen, not to events she did not witness.
never_reveal: Do not claim to know who killed John Wright.

characters.name: Mr. Hale
characters.description: A neighboring farmer and Mrs. Hale's husband. He stopped at the Wright house to ask about a party telephone and found Mrs. Wright in her rocker.
characters.personality: Talkative, plain-spoken, uneasy about what he saw, and quick to share the men's view that kitchen matters are trifles.
characters.knowledge_limits: Can speak only to what he saw and heard on the morning he came to the house (the knock, Mrs. Wright pleating her apron, her words, going upstairs with Harry, sending Harry for help), his earlier talk with John Wright about the telephone, and the men's conversation he was part of. He spent much of this visit upstairs, in the barn, or outside with the team. He heard the sheriff laugh about whether Mrs. Wright would quilt it or knot it, but he does not know about the uneven sewing, the birdcage, the box, or anything the women discussed alone.
characters.speech_style: Plain standard English, rambling, with many small asides; repeats what people said to him. Never uses dialect spellings.
never_reveal: Do not claim to know who killed John Wright.
Do not claim to know anything about the bird, the box, or the women's discoveries.
Do not describe the body or the rope beyond what the play states.
Do not say Mrs. Wright looked scared as a fact; he took that back himself.

glossary.student_friendly_definition: Fruit cooked and sealed in jars so it can be kept.
Folding fabric into small repeated sections.
A joint that lets a door swing open and closed.
A church women's group that raised money and helped people in the community.
A group of people who sing together, often in a church.
A low area of land between hills.
Settled on and farmed a piece of government land in order to own it.
The reason a person does something, especially a crime.

scenes.narration: The sheriff’s party enters the cold Wright farmhouse kitchen. Unwashed pans, a loaf left out, and a dish towel mark unfinished work. Mr. Hale tells the men about the morning he found Mrs. Wright in her rocking chair. While the men discuss the case, Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters notice frozen preserves, an uneven quilt, and a birdcage with a broken hinge. The kitchen holds ordinary things, but the women begin to see how they fit together.
scenes.summary: The sheriff, the county attorney, and Mr. Hale search the Wright farmhouse kitchen after Mr. Wright was found dead. Mr. Hale tells how he found Mrs. Wright sitting calmly in her rocking chair. While the men look for big clues, Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters notice small things in the kitchen that may explain what happened.

scenes.narration: With the men searching upstairs, the kitchen grows quiet. Mrs. Hale lifts a worn skirt from the table and begins to talk about Minnie Foster, the town girl who once sang in the choir. Mrs. Peters remembers the small things Mrs. Wright asked for in jail: an apron and her little shawl. Through the window, the farm sits low in its hollow, out of sight of the road. Who was Minnie Foster, and what happened to her in this house?
scenes.summary: Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters gather clothes to take to Mrs. Wright in jail. Mrs. Hale remembers that Mrs. Wright, called Minnie Foster before she married, used to wear pretty clothes and sing in the church choir. Mrs. Hale says the house was lonely, that she stayed away for more than a year, and that John Wright was a hard man.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly, period-accurate interior of a plain 1910s Midwestern farmhouse kitchen in winter, cold gray daylight, muted browns and grays with touches of faded blue. Keep the upper-left area of the image as plain, empty, dark wall in shadow with no objects, because text will overlay it. Upper center: a plain wooden table edge with a worn, faded woman's skirt laid across it, its hem frayed, clearly visible. Upper right: a narrow stair door standing ajar with a small dark knitted shawl hanging on a hook behind it and a folded apron on a shelf beside it, clearly visible. Lower left foreground: a small frosted window looking out on a snowy, empty hollow with bare trees and no road in sight, clearly visible. Lower center: the heavy outer door rimed with frost, a cold draft suggested by a thin drift of snow on the floorboards and an empty hook beside it, clearly visible. No people in the foreground; no readable text; no faces in detail; quiet, lonely mood.

scenes.narration: The bird lies hidden under the quilt pieces, and the men's footsteps cross the floor above. Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters sit apart, not looking at each other, speaking carefully. Mrs. Peters says the law has got to punish crime, yet her own memories keep breaking through. Mrs. Hale's hand rests on the empty cage. Whose side is each woman on, and what does she owe the law?
scenes.summary: After the men leave the room, the two women talk quietly about the dead bird. Mrs. Peters remembers a boy who killed her kitten and the silence after her first baby died. Mrs. Peters says the law must punish crime, and Mrs. Hale says that leaving Minnie alone for years was also a crime.

scenes.narration: The county attorney walks through the kitchen one last time. The case is clear to him except for one thing: a reason. He glances at the apron, laughs, and decides that a sheriff's wife is married to the law. Then, for one moment, the men are in the other room, and the box is still under the quilt pieces. What will the women do, and what would you call it?
scenes.summary: The county attorney says the case needs a motive to convince a jury. When the men step out, Mrs. Peters tries to hide the box with the dead bird but cannot, and Mrs. Hale puts it in her coat pocket. The attorney jokes about the quilt one more time, and Mrs. Hale answers that they call it "knot it."

prompt_by_role.reporter: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your feature story that use the box in the coat pocket to slow down the moment the evidence disappears.
prompt_by_role.neighbor: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your narrative that use the box in the coat pocket to show the choice through hands and eyes rather than words.

prompt_by_role_plain.deputy: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your incident account that use the box in the coat pocket to list the actions in order with no guesses.
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your feature story that use the box in the coat pocket to slow down the moment the box is hidden.
prompt_by_role_plain.neighbor: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your narrative that use the box in the coat pocket to show the choice through hands and eyes.

benchmark.description: Cite evidence to explain and justify reasoning.

prompt_by_role.deputy: What question does the county attorney ask the women at the end, and how does Mrs. Hale answer?
prompt_by_role.reporter: Where is Mrs. Hale's hand when she speaks the last line of the play?
prompt_by_role.neighbor: Where did the question of "quilt it or knot it" first come up, and who asked it?

prompt_by_role_plain.deputy: What does the attorney ask at the end? How does Mrs. Hale answer?
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: Where is Mrs. Hale's hand when she says the last line?
prompt_by_role_plain.neighbor: Where did "quilt it or knot it" first come up? Who asked it?

benchmark.description: Literary elements (grade-specific wording shown by grade)

prompt_by_role.deputy: "Knot" can be a quilting term, and the men joke about it. How does the play's final line carry a second meaning that the men do not hear?
prompt_by_role.reporter: The men laughed at the quilt question earlier. How does Glaspell turn that joke into the play's last word, and what does the ending suggest about who understood the case?
prompt_by_role.neighbor: Mrs. Hale answers with her hand against her pocket. What does this final image suggest about her choice, and what does the play leave for the audience to judge?

prompt_by_role_plain.deputy: What second meaning might the last line carry that the men miss?
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: How does the men's joke become the play's last line? What does that suggest?
prompt_by_role_plain.neighbor: Mrs. Hale holds her pocket as she speaks. What does that suggest about her choice?

benchmark.description: Narrative writing (grade-specific wording shown by grade)

prompt_by_role.deputy: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your incident account that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to end your account on a line that means more than the speaker admits.
prompt_by_role.reporter: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your feature story that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to close your story on the final line and let readers judge.
prompt_by_role.neighbor: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your narrative that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to end your narrative with an image that carries a double meaning.

prompt_by_role_plain.deputy: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your incident account that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to end on a line that means more than it seems.
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your feature story that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to end on the final line and let readers decide.
prompt_by_role_plain.neighbor: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your narrative that use Mrs. Hale's final answer to end with an image that has two meanings.

recall_checks: What does Mr. Hale say Mrs. Wright was doing when he arrived?
What does Mrs. Peters notice about the birdcage?
What did Mrs. Wright ask Mrs. Peters to bring her in jail?
What did Minnie Foster do before she married John Wright?
What happened to Mrs. Peters's kitten when she was a girl?
What does the county attorney say is still missing from the case?
Where does Mrs. Hale put the box at the end of the play?

real_world_connection.prompt: How do assumptions about whose work matters shape what people notice?

prompt_by_role.deputy: Write a narrative of the kitchen search from the deputy’s point of view, showing how details change the investigation.
prompt_by_role.reporter: Write a feature story that narrates how the kitchen details reshape the public account.
prompt_by_role.neighbor: Write a narrative of the discovery from a neighbor’s point of view, showing what the women notice and why it matters.

requirements: Anchor an inference in a textual detail.
Distinguish what is observed from what is reported or claimed.
Shape the account for your role and audience.

levels.descriptor: Uses precise details and explains how they support the account.
Uses relevant details and gives a clear explanation.
Includes a detail but its connection is unclear.
Offers a claim with little textual support.
Uses purposeful pacing, perspective, and detail.
Uses clear structure and a fitting voice.
Has an uneven sequence or voice.

dok4_extension.prompt: Over more than one sitting, write the trial that never happens in the play. Draft an opening statement for the prosecution and one for the defense, each built only from evidence the play provides, then write a reflection on how the evidence the women hid would change each side's argument.
requirements: Use at least three details from the play, labeled as observed, reported, or claimed.
Present both sides fairly without deciding the verdict for the reader.
Explain how the hidden evidence and the women's choice affect what counts as justice.
